name: Hana Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, AI companies, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play saxophone in a theatre jazz band, record short horn lines and teach five pupils. I have a music bachelor’s and enough years to lead a section rehearsal, though I am a solid working player rather than a solo name. I like the breath before a band entrance; I dislike chasing the recording fee after the show.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do those calls mean for home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, my partner is an electrician and our children are grown. We have a mortgage and eleven months of expenses saved; my theatre and recording fees are high for this work, and there are many music employers nearby. I use AI every day for rough schedules and to sort my own rehearsal notes, then check every paid time and keep pupil audio private.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that a faster schedule is welcome if every horn player’s fee is on it. I would still check the calls with the stage manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre run, five pupils and my partner’s work cover our mortgage. Eleven months saved handles an ordinary cancelled session without forcing a household cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep paid band dates, horn recordings and five pupils, and get the next run’s rehearsal and cancellation fees in writing. In the first plateau year I would request my actual pension estimate before choosing a retirement date and save one fifth of cleared extra horn fees after mortgage, food and travel toward twelve months of bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this income. A paid horn call is worth more than a screen full of enquiries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in a schedule?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fee, start time and travel between venues. An AI draft is just a draft until it matches the signed call sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not read a pension estimate. My partner and I would compare the actual figure with our mortgage before setting a date.

think: Current **theatre and electrical work** pays the mortgage.

do: Keep **band, recordings and pupils** with written rehearsal and cancellation fees.
Request **actual pension estimate**; save fifth of cleared extra horn fees after essentials toward twelve months.
feel: I feel **calm** about current fees and bills.

fieldNote: Her **eleven-month reserve** and high paid season support a calm plateau.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the band manager which recorded horn lines are still paid. I would tell colleagues that a live saxophone section still listens to the cast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect some advert buyers to use generated horns, and those short sessions make about a quarter of my own income. Eleven months saved buys time, but it does not make that pay reappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep paid theatre dates and five pupils and ask for written recording rates. If two monthly horn calls disappear, I would seek a posted paid school jazz-ensemble lead role only if my music bachelor’s and section-leading experience meet its requirements, actual live teaching hours remain paid, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the route works; I would keep current music until a signed offer during disruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real recording line shrinking. Several schools may hire nearby, but I still need a posted vacancy with the right pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could AI finish your recordings for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use AI for notes, not a pupil’s voice or another player’s track without permission. I would check any proposed musical change by ear before delivery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a school title with fewer paid hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would read the actual live teaching and preparation hours before leaving the band. A title cannot replace a session fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that 2028 thinking AGI could book and make horn tracks before robot saxophonists arrive around 2031. I would ask for signed live dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect advert horn calls to end and some rehearsal preparation fees to go in 2028. That cuts my own income noticeably, although the paid theatre chair may last longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Before 2028 I would get signed theatre dates and keep five pupils. In the first year after 2028, if horn calls end and preparation pay falls, I would seek a posted paid school jazz-ensemble lead job only if my music bachelor’s and section-leading work qualify, real live teaching and preparation hours remain paid, written net pay after travel replaces lost income and the route fits; I would keep band and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the speed of lost recording money. Eleven months saved and many nearby employers let me compare real openings, not assume a school will have one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could school rehearsals become automated too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They might. I would read the posted duties and paid hours; I would not treat live teaching as guaranteed work just because the title sounds musical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why plan before robot players?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card places capable robot saxophonists around 2031. Booking and recorded music can lose buyers in 2028, and that is the first invoice risk.

do: Keep **band and pupils** with signed dates before 2028 until signed offer.
Seek **posted jazz lead** after both horn/prep losses; music bachelor’s/section leadership accepted, paid live teaching/preparation.
Require **written replacement net** after travel and a workable route before any school move.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a noticeable cut to my pay.
S2.quote: I would not treat live teaching as guaranteed work just because the title sounds musical.
fieldNote: The **2028 loss** reaches bookings and horn recordings before robot playing.
The **school role** must post real paid live duties and a written net wage replacing lost sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that five years lets us ask what live horn work and sound checks pay. Thinking AGI arrives around 2031 and robot saxophonists around 2034 in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Advert calls may fade before the stage does. I could learn live sound, but an unfunded certificate would cost paid lessons and prove nothing to a hiring venue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep the band and five pupils and check posted paid sound-assistant jobs. If two monthly advert calls disappear, I would enrol in a live-sound certificate only after a real funded place pays training hours, a posting recognises the certificate before enrolment, and the timetable preserves current paid band calls, lessons and travel; in the first year after 2031 I would move only to that posted paid role on a signed written net offer after travel replacing lost fees, with a workable route, keeping music until then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about recording pay over the next few years. Five years before AGI in 2031 lets me check a paid live-sound course and job offer without spending mortgage reserves on a brochure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you run a crowded sound desk alone after class?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. A venue technician would supervise my first checks, and I would wait for signed equipment and safety clearance before handling a crowded show alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course covers tuition but not hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not enrol. Paid training hours and my existing pupil income must survive the timetable, or I keep the music work I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my grown children that thinking AGI around 2036 and robot saxophonists around 2039 are different dates. I would still ask what a recorded horn use pays today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may prefer fewer late theatre shows, but I have no retirement date without an actual pension estimate. Eleven months saved and current household wages make the next few years secure, not the whole decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would keep band dates and five pupils, request my actual pension estimate and save one fifth of cleared extra recording fees after mortgage, food and travel toward twelve months. Across the decade I would ask for written recorded-use rates; in the first year after 2036, if horn and preparation fees fall, I would seek a posted paid school jazz-ensemble lead role only if my music bachelor’s and section-leading experience qualify, actual paid live teaching and preparation remain, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and transport works, keeping current music until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant recording work while present bookings and my partner’s wage hold the mortgage. A decade is useful for gathering contracts, not for counting imagined pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count pension money now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would request the actual estimate and compare it with our bills before naming any retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the school has no live post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid band and pupils while dates last and check other posted vacancies. I would not leave paid band work for a school jazz job that exists only on a forecast.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because horn sessions and preparation could lose fees before another role pays. Signed theatre dates, an actual school post paying live teaching and written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns a recorded horn line when a client uses it again. A player can breathe into a microphone once and hear that note sold a hundred times.

headlineQuote: A player can breathe into a microphone once and hear that note sold a hundred times.
portrait: Hana is an **experienced saxophonist** with a music bachelor’s, five pupils and high theatre fees.
She has **eleven months saved**, an electrician partner, grown children and a mortgage.
She uses **AI daily** for draft schedules and notes, checking paid calls and pupil privacy.
She considers **funded live-sound training** only after actual recording loss, with a recognised certificate and paid time.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could cut horn and preparation fees before another paid role is available.
whatWouldHelp: She needs **signed theatre dates**, an actual paid live school role and written replacement net after travel.
